How to Deploy and Commission the Metering System

Commissioning is where good hardware turns into defensible billing data, and it's the stage vendors compress hardest when an installation runs behind. Push back. A meter that's mounted but not verified is a liability with a serial number.

children.text: The sequence that survives an audit
1. Inventory every meter against the floor plan.

List each utility meter, unit, common area and shared load, and reconcile the list to the building footprint. A missed meter becomes an unallocated cost that the owner absorbs for years. The usual slip is a spare meter or a shared-load meter nobody claimed.
2. Confirm the equipment against the design.

Check model numbers, CT or PT ratios and the wiring diagram before anything is mounted, because a ratio error skews every reading that follows for the life of the installation. The slip is copying ratios from the last building because the panel looked similar.
3. Install at accessible heights and label everything.

Every meter gets its number and service address on a durable label, readable without a ladder or a torch. A unit mislabelled with the wrong address is worse than no label, because the error flows straight into a resident's invoice.
4. Verify phase association and CT polarity.

Reversed polarity is the most common field failure, and it produces plausible-looking data that overstates or understates consumption depending on load balance. Confirm orientation with a load test rather than trusting the arrow printed on the CT.
5. Synchronise clocks to a common time source.

Then confirm interval counts, units and billing-window alignment against the specification. Devices on different time sources misalign billing windows, which shows up later as a demand peak that never happened.
6. Compare submeter totals with the parent meter.

Record the comparison during a stable load and again at peak, and investigate any interval where the sum of submeters exceeds the parent. Comparing only at low load hides ratio and polarity errors that appear under real demand.
7. Set acceptance thresholds below the stated field tolerance.

An escalation level set above the tolerance lets a failing meter pass acceptance, and you'll spend the next year explaining variances. Keep pre- and post-commissioning test records with the serial numbers attached.
8. Sign off before billing starts.

The property manager and the vendor both countersign a sheet listing every meter, its assigned unit, its interval count and its variance result. That single page is the difference between a billing dispute you can answer in an hour and one you argue about for a quarter.
Practical rule:
if a meter's variance sits inside tolerance but its label, address or assignment is wrong, the meter is still failing.

Two administrative habits save trouble later. Photograph every installed meter with its label and CT orientation, and file the images against the meter register. Then hand the property manager a one-page map of what was installed, because the person answering a resident's question in eighteen months won't be the person who stood in the electrical room.
Connecting Meter Data to Billing and Operations

Trace the path before you trust it: meter, collector or concentrator, head-end system, data store, then billing and reporting tools. Each junction has a characteristic failure. A collector stops reporting and the gap fills with a repeat of the previous day. A head-end export drops a column and the upload imports zeroes. A billing tool applies the wrong rate period because the interval timestamps shifted an hour.

The monthly routine that catches all three is unglamorous. Check every meter for missing intervals, duplicated records and abnormal demand peaks. Sum the submeters and compare the total against the utility statement for the same period. Log every correction with its reason, date and approver, so the audit trail shows a decision rather than a mystery.
Monitoring data should not drive tenant allocation, savings claims or operating decisions until that month's completeness check has passed.
Completeness is an owner obligation, not a vendor promise. The
California Energy Commission's building energy benchmarking program

warns that benchmarking submissions may omit meters associated with the building, notes that utility data can be requested or uploaded into ENERGY STAR Portfolio Manager, and sets reporting for covered commercial and multifamily properties generally due by June 1 for the prior calendar year. State reporting aggregates whole-building use, and no automatic mechanism confirms every associated meter was included. If the completeness check runs only when a report is due, the omission surfaces after the deadline.

Billing runs should freeze on a rule, not on a date. Run the reconciliation first, then freeze the cycle, then hold any unit that fails until its exception clears. Holding one invoice for two days costs less than issuing a correction credit and rebuilding a resident's trust.

Mixed-use buildings need separate billing groups for residential, commercial and shared loads so one class never inherits another's errors. Connect the system to property accounting and to the maintenance ticketing queue as well, because a fault or leak alert that only appears on a dashboard nobody watches becomes a work order three weeks late.

Submeter-to-parent variance tells you whether the equipment is still inside tolerance or has drifted since commissioning, which is a hardware question rather than a billing one. Estimated-read share and dispute rate are the two resident-facing measures, and they move together: a rising estimate share almost always drags disputes up a month or two later.

Cost recovery deserves a plain calculation. Compare billed submetered cost against the utility cost for the same period. If the programme recovers less than the utility charges, the shortfall lands on the owner's operating statement, and it usually traces to unallocated common loads rather than to rates.

Fault response time is the measure that exposes a service agreement in practice. Compare the hours from alert to technician visit against what the contract promised, and review it quarterly with the vendor rather than annually in a renewal meeting.

Consumption change needs patience. Compare post-installation use against the baseline under similar weather, because a single mild month will flatter any programme. Then set the review rhythm: monthly for reconciliation and billing, quarterly for service performance and consumption, annually for vendor performance against the contract.
Any KPI outside target for two consecutive months goes to a named owner with a fix date, not onto a slide.
Protecting Residents From Billing Errors and Arrears

An accurate meter can still lead to an unfair bill if an estimate is presented as a confirmed reading, a dispute has no clear route, or arrears notices omit repayment options. Protecting residents depends on the process around the data as much as the measurement itself.

body.alt: A woman looks at her electricity bill on her smartphone while standing next to a smart meter.

children.text: Label estimated reads plainly on the invoice and explain why an estimate was used. When actual data becomes available, adjust the account and show the correction as a separate line. That lets residents distinguish an estimate from a measured consumption figure and follow how the balance changed.

Set up the dispute route before the first billing cycle. Define how residents submit complaints, how quickly the team responds, and how staff check interval data against the audit trail. Test the process with a sample case: an estimated bill is labelled, the resident submits a written dispute, staff review the data, and any error results in a corrected invoice. If a balance remains unpaid, apply the relevant notice and repayment process before considering any service limitation.
Ontario's Unit Sub-Metering Code amendments, effective
August 18, 2025
, require stronger disclosure of consumer-protection policies, including
arrears-payment agreements, winter disconnection and reconnection policies, and reconnection charges
, according to the
Ontario Gazette government notices

. Billing based on suite-meter consumption must also comply with the Energy Consumer Protection Act, Ontario Energy Board requirements, and applicable codes. Put these policies in resident-facing documents, where residents can find them, rather than leaving them only in a management contract.

The Ontario requirements apply in Ontario. Elsewhere, confirm local rules before drafting resident documents. Disconnection and repayment conditions vary by jurisdiction, so a template from another market can create compliance risk.
A monitoring system earns trust through a defensible exception and dispute process, not through dashboard refresh speed alone.

Label estimated reads plainly on the invoice and explain why an estimate was used. When actual data becomes available, adjust the account and show the correction as a separate line. That lets residents distinguish an estimate from a measured consumption figure and follow how the balance changed.

Set up the dispute route before the first billing cycle. Define how residents submit complaints, how quickly the team responds, and how staff check interval data against the audit trail. Test the process with a sample case: an estimated bill is labelled, the resident submits a written dispute, staff review the data, and any error results in a corrected invoice. If a balance remains unpaid, apply the relevant notice and repayment process before considering any service limitation.

Ontario's Unit Sub-Metering Code amendments, effective August 18, 2025, require stronger disclosure of consumer-protection policies, including arrears-payment agreements, winter disconnection and reconnection policies, and reconnection charges, according to the Ontario Gazette government notices. Billing based on suite-meter consumption must also comply with the Energy Consumer Protection Act, Ontario Energy Board requirements, and applicable codes. Put these policies in resident-facing documents, where residents can find them, rather than leaving them only in a management contract.

The Ontario requirements apply in Ontario. Elsewhere, confirm local rules before drafting resident documents. Disconnection and repayment conditions vary by jurisdiction, so a template from another market can create compliance risk.

A monitoring system earns trust through a defensible exception and dispute process, not through dashboard refresh speed alone.

For practical guidance on invoice structure and tenant charges, see how to bill tenants for utilities. Align the dispute and adjustment workflow with the billing process before the first cycle.
